newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Bucharest bourse loses steam but stays on track.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bucharest bourse loses steam but stays on track.

text.p: The Bucharest bourse, bolstered by strong buying interest in the New Year, has since lost its vigour as foreign investors return to the sidelines in the absence of signs of investor-friendly legislation.
Analysts say a combination of factors, including a firmer leu and other, more attractive opportunities for local investors are also discouraging equity investment.

"Recent statements by government members, which showed a lack of clarity as concerns portfolio investment, made some foreign buyers withdraw orders from the market," said Marcel Cobuz, executive president of Creditanstalt Securities.
Brokers, analysts and bourse officials agree Romania needs clear rules on portfolio flows and on the repatriation of initial investment and capital gains.
"Such rules are pivotal for the growth of the capital market," said stock exchange general manager Stere Farmache.
Analysts also say that to extend its recovery the bourse needs higher liquidity and less volatility. They blame a change in the rules allowing price variations of 50 percent, instead of 10 percent.
"In the absence of company news, the change made the market more volatile and scared off investors," said one analyst.

The existing foreign investment law covers only direct investment and no institution is authorised to issue portfolio investor certificates to serve in repatriation-related foreign exchange operations.

Portfolio investors who pumped money into Romanian equities will be able to move their gains out of the country only when the leu currency -- now convertible for current account operations -- becomes fully convertible.
"Foreign buyers took that chance thanks to the obvious commitment to reforms of the new government," said a broker.
The centrist government coalition, in power since former leftists lost last November's elections, has repeatedly promised to back capital market growth and foreign investment.
BUCHAREST BOURSE GRADUALLY LOST GLAMOUR
The strong performance at the start of the year was a welcome change from sluggish behaviour through most of 1996.
Taking heart from government promises of a liberalised market, local institutional investors and foreign buyers rushed to buy Romanian equities.
Volumes and prices drifted higher for almost two months and turnover per session hit an all-time high of 6.3 billion lei ($933,000) in mid-February. The previous record was 1.7 billion last March.
"The mood was good, despite liquidity which remains low in comparison with other countries in the area and focused on the first-tier stocks," said a broker.

The Bucharest bourse trades 26 stocks, but only two on the first tier, which normally take over 80 percent of turnover. Market capitalisation is the equivalent of around $70 million, with an average free float of some 45 percent.

"With the appreciation of the leu we gradually lost foreign investors as the new rates made stocks more expensive," a Bucharest trader said. "And smaller domestic investors started to prefer banks to the bourse."
Tough monetary policies pushed the leu up to some 7,000 to the dollar, after a slump which sent it spiralling to 9,000 from 4,000 in the New Year.
The tighter steps also hoisted leu deposit rates to an annual 150 percent from 50 percent early in the year, driving money flows away from the bourse and into high-return deposits.
BROKERS OPTIMISTIC ABOUT FUTURE PROSPECTS
Traded volumes on the bourse began sliding in recent sessions, with turnover revolving round 1.5 billion lei.
But brokers remain optimistic.

"The government has a programme to set privatisation spinning, which will increase market liquidity. In the long run, we also have chances of a stable leu," another trader said. "What we need fast are portfolio rules."
The government met investors half-way, drafting amendments to current legislation to include portfolio investment.

The draft allows for free repatriation of initial investment and capital gains. The tax on gains repatriation is 18 percent, except for capital gains withdrawn sooner than a year, when the charge is 28 percent.
Capital gains will be repatriated only in the currency in which the initial investment was made, the draft says.
Most Romanian brokers are pleased with the draft, but say it will take a long time before it wins approval from the government and clears parliament.
Economic Reform Minister Ulm Spineanu could not say when the draft was expected to become law, but said parliament would deal with it as an urgent priority.

"This will not happen before next year. The government doesn't really favour portfolio investors because they are afraid of their volatile movement," said Murat Bahcivanoglu, an equity analyst with Caspian Securities Ltd in London.
"They do not want volatility because the equilibrium of the economy is fragile," said Bahcivanoglu, recently in Bucharest for a conference on investment opportunities.

As foreign exchange market liberalisation, tight monetary and fiscal policies and privatisation plans start bearing fruit, investor confidence in Romania is expected to swell. But risks remain, including currency and market volatility.

Romania gained its first credit rating last year, but failed to win an investment grade. It was awarded a BB-minus by Standard & Poor's and IBCA, a Ba-three from Moody's Investor Service and a BB-plus from Japan Credit Rating Agency.
"If problems are solved, waves of investment are to be expected as Romania promises to sell well in 1997," Cobuz said. ($ = 6750 Romanian Lei)
